title: Two days of headache, fever and neck stiffness in a 32-year-old teacher on prednisolone
desc: This station has a focused history and examination of a 32-year-old high school teacher in the ED. He has had 2 days of a worsening generalised headache with fever, neck stiffness, vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia after a recent viral illness. He has been taking prednisolone since an asthma admission last month and has a penicillin allergy. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, bloods, CT brain report and CSF results. They then manage bacterial meningitis in an immunosuppressed patient according to eTG, including Listeria cover that takes his allergy into account and steroid cover. Finally they answer his questions about COVID and whether his girlfriend can catch it.
focus: Headache with fever and meningism in an immunosuppressed patient: recognising bacterial meningitis, treating without delay and adjusting empirical therapy for corticosteroid use and penicillin allergy
stem: You are the junior medical officer in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Ned Wallace, a 32-year-old high school teacher, has come in with a headache. He is lying on a trolley in an acute bay with monitoring attached. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Ned and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think he needs as you go (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Ned's observations, blood results, CT brain report and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Ned Wallace, 32, a high school teacher. You feel awful. You lie still with your eyes half shut, wince at bright light and loud noise, and move your head as little as possible. You are fully alert and answer clearly, but slowly and with effort. If the candidate dims the lights, keeps the bay quiet, or gives you something for the pain or the nausea, you settle a little and say so (“That's a bit better, thanks”). The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “My head is killing me. It's been going for two days and it just keeps getting worse.”

The headache (give only when asked)

  • Site: all over your head, generalised. It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • Onset: it came on suddenly, out of nowhere, 2 days ago in the afternoon while you were at school. If asked whether it hit you like a blow to the head or was at its worst within a minute: “No, it came on out of nowhere that afternoon, but it's got worse since.” If asked if it is the worst headache of your life: “It's bad, but my worst migraines have been as bad. It's the fever and the stiff neck that are different.”
  • Character: a dull ache.
  • Time course: constant for 2 days and getting worse.
  • Severity: 7/10. “I feel like it's affecting the way I think.” If asked what you mean: you find it hard to concentrate because of the pain. You know where you are, what day it is and what is happening, and nobody has said you are confused.
  • Worse with: bright light and loud sound.
  • Better with: lying in a quiet, dark room. Paracetamol at home barely touched it.

Previous headaches (give when asked)

  • You have had migraines before, a few times a year since your teens. They are throbbing, on one side, sometimes with zigzag lines first, and gone within a day after sleep.
  • “This one feels different. It's all over, it won't go away and I feel sick and hot with it.”

Other symptoms (give when asked)

  • Fever: you have been hot and sweaty, with shivers last night.
  • Neck: your neck is stiff and painful to bend forward. This started yesterday.
  • Nausea and vomiting: you feel sick all the time and have vomited 3 times today, with no blood. You have not eaten much and have been drinking less.
  • Recent illness: you have been feeling pretty under the weather for about a week, with a sore throat and a runny nose. Lots of the kids at school have had colds.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No rash or spots anywhere.
  • No fits, no blackouts, no confusion and no drowsiness. Mia (your girlfriend) has not said you are acting oddly.
  • No collapse or passing out when it started.
  • No head injury or fall.
  • No weakness, numbness or pins and needles, no slurred speech, no trouble walking, no dizziness or spinning.
  • No blurred or double vision and no loss of vision. No red or watering eye, no one-sided blocked or running nostril and no drooping eyelid with the headache (your runny nose from the cold was both sides and has settled).
  • It is not worse first thing in the morning, or on lying down, coughing or straining.
  • No band-like tightness and no unusual stress at work. No jaw pain on chewing and no scalp tenderness.
  • No cough or shortness of breath beyond your usual asthma. No ear or sinus pain. No burning when passing urine.
  • No overseas or interstate travel. As far as you know your vaccinations are up to date, but you are not sure about a meningococcal vaccine.

Past medical history

  • Asthma since childhood. Last month you were admitted to hospital with a bad attack and were given prednisolone.
  • Kidney stones, removed with a laser a few years ago.

Medications

  • Ventolin puffer when needed, a few times a week.
  • Oral prednisolone every morning since the admission. “No one told me when to stop, so I've just kept taking it.” You are not sure of the dose (“a few small tablets”).
  • A multivitamin.

Allergies

  • Penicillin: rash. If asked for more detail: an itchy red rash all over as a child after amoxicillin, which settled in a few days. No swelling of the lips or tongue, no breathing trouble, no blistering or peeling skin and no hospital stay.

Family history

  • Your mother has Graves' disease and had a thyroidectomy 10 years ago.
  • Your father had a heart attack 5 years ago. He is alive and well.
  • Your brother has eczema and hayfever.

Social history

  • You smoke 5 to 8 cigarettes a day and have done for 5 years.
  • A glass of white wine a few times a week. No recreational drugs.
  • You have been a high school teacher for 5 years. You go to the gym twice a week and eat out often.
  • You live near the city with your girlfriend of 15 years, Mia, who is your main support. Your brother lives an hour away.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: “I feel like it could be some infection, as I've been feeling pretty under the weather recently. Could be something I've picked up from the kids at school.”
  • Concerns: “I'm worried that it could be COVID related.” “I've had to stop teaching and take some sick leave.”
  • Expectations: you want something for the headache and to know what is going on.
  • Question to ask (once, towards the end): “Do you think it's COVID?”

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • Gives the observations and a bedside glucose when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If the candidate orders anything (cannula, bloods, blood cultures, fluids, analgesia, antiemetic, dexamethasone, antibiotics, CT, lumbar puncture), says “I'll get that started.” If a drug is ordered without a dose or route, asks “What dose and route would you like?”
  • If an antibiotic is ordered before the candidate has asked about allergies, asks: “Has he got any allergies?” Ned then answers as above.
  • If the candidate asks for a CT brain, asks once: “Do you want to wait for the CT before the antibiotics?” Let the candidate answer.
  • If the candidate has not ordered any treatment or investigations by halfway, says: “He looks really unwell. Is there anything you'd like me to do?”
  • If the candidate asks for blood, CT or CSF results, says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: flushed, sweaty and unwell, lying still with his eyes half closed. Photophobic. Weight 78 kg.
  • Observations: RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 118/72, HR 112 regular, temperature 38.9 °C, CRT 2 seconds, pain 7/10. Bedside glucose 8.6 mmol/L.
  • Conscious state: GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6). Oriented to time, place and person. Attention intact (says the months of the year backwards correctly).
  • Skin: no rash, no petechiae and no purpura anywhere, including the trunk, legs, palms, soles and conjunctivae.
  • Meningism: marked neck stiffness (resists passive neck flexion). Kernig's sign positive. Brudzinski's sign positive. Photophobia.
  • Fundoscopy: sharp optic discs, no papilloedema.
  • Cranial nerves: pupils 4 mm, equal and reactive. Visual fields full. Eye movements full, no diplopia or nystagmus. Face symmetrical. Hearing normal to whisper. Palate and tongue normal.
  • Limbs: tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. No pronator drift. Coordination normal. Plantars flexor. Gait not tested (too unwell to stand).
  • Head, ears, nose and throat: no signs of head injury. Tympanic membranes normal. Throat mildly red, no exudate. Sinuses not tender. Dry mucous membranes.
  • Cardiovascular: HR 112 regular, heart sounds dual, no murmur. Peripheries warm.
  • Respiratory: chest clear, no wheeze.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender. No renal angle tenderness.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Ned's identity and gains consent before examining.
Recognises an unwell patient: acknowledges his pain, dims the lights and keeps the bay quiet, offers analgesia and an antiemetic early, uses plain language and keeps the history focused.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Site, character and severity: generalised, dull ache, 7/10
Onset and course: out of nowhere 2 days ago in the afternoon, constant and getting worse
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse with bright light and loud sound, better lying in a quiet dark room; paracetamol barely helped

check.x: Elicits the features of meningitis: fever with sweats and shivers, neck stiffness, nausea with vomiting 3 times today, and photophobia and phonophobia.
Specifically asks about a rash (none).

Asks about a recent infection, sick contacts, travel and vaccination: a week under the weather with sore throat and runny nose, unwell children at school, no travel, unsure about a meningococcal vaccine.
Screens for other dangerous causes of headache:

kids.x: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: clarifies the 'sudden' onset was not a thunderclap (not maximal within a minute), not worst-ever, no collapse
Encephalitis: asks about confusion, drowsiness, behaviour change and seizures, and clarifies that 'affecting the way I think' means poor concentration, not confusion
Raised intracranial pressure or stroke: headache worse in the morning or on lying, coughing or straining; focal weakness, speech or visual change

check.x: Asks about his previous migraines and how this headache differs (all over, constant, with fever), and screens for tension-type (band-like, stress) and cluster headache (one-sided eye pain, tearing, nasal symptoms).
Identifies that he is immunosuppressed by corticosteroids:

kids.x: Asthma since childhood, admitted last month with a bad attack and given prednisolone
Still taking oral prednisolone every day since the admission, unsure of the dose and never told when to stop, and plans to confirm the dose (discharge summary, community pharmacy or My Health Record)

check.x: Takes the rest of the past history and medications: kidney stones removed by laser, Ventolin as needed, multivitamin.
Asks about allergies before any antibiotic is given and characterises the penicillin reaction: a childhood rash with no angioedema, breathing difficulty, blistering or mucosal involvement.
Briefly asks about family history.
Brief social history including smoking, alcohol, occupation and who is at home (Mia).
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is an infection from the children at school, worried it is COVID, has had to take sick leave, wants relief and an explanation.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations and a bedside glucose, and notes the fever of 38.9 °C, HR 112 and a glucose of 8.6 mmol/L.
Assesses conscious state by GCS components (E4 V5 M6 = 15) and orientation, and checks the pupils.
Inspects the whole skin for a petechial or purpuric (non-blanching) rash.
Examines for meningism and finds marked neck stiffness with positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs.
Looks for focal signs and raised intracranial pressure: fundoscopy (no papilloedema), cranial nerves and a limb neurological screen, all normal.
Assesses hydration and looks for a source in at least three areas: mucous membranes and CRT, ears, throat and sinuses, chest, abdomen.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: the temperature is in the yellow zone from arrival. By 17:10 RR 26, systolic BP 96, HR 126 and temperature 39.4 °C are all in the yellow zone, with CRT 3 seconds and the nurse concerned. States that this is worsening sepsis needing senior escalation now, with ICU review, and a rapid response for any red zone value or a fall in GCS. With multiple yellow zone values and nurse concern, calling a rapid response now under local CERS criteria is also appropriate; accept either an urgent senior clinical review or a rapid response call.
Interprets the bloods: neutrophilia, CRP 214 and lactate 3.1 with a metabolic acidosis show sepsis with hypoperfusion; SARS-CoV-2 not detected.
Interprets the CT brain: no mass, haemorrhage, hydrocephalus, oedema or shift, so there was no contraindication to the LP.
Interprets the CSF:

kids.x: Turbid fluid, raised opening pressure, neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose (calculates a CSF:plasma ratio of about 0.17): a bacterial pattern

No organisms on Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis (especially after antibiotics); culture and PCR are pending, so empirical cover continues, including Listeria; may note the negative cryptococcal antigen and minimal red cells
kids.d: The cryptococcal antigen and red cell comments are optional and not needed for the mark.

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as bacterial meningitis with sepsis in a patient immunosuppressed by corticosteroids, supported by fever, headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and phonophobia, and the CSF.
Names at least three differentials, each with a feature against it, from: viral meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, migraine, tension-type headache, stroke.
Management
In Part 1, once fever and neck stiffness are found, asks the nurse for blood cultures and immediate dexamethasone and IV antibiotics, without waiting for CT or LP.
check.d: Part 1 item. Credit only if ordered during Part 1.

check.x: Resuscitates and escalates: ABCDE assessment, senior ED doctor now, IV access, IV crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL to 1 L Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 to 30 minutes, per the local sepsis pathway) with reassessment of BP, HR, CRT, urine output and lactate, ICU review.

Orders the work-up: BGL, FBC, UEC, LFT, CRP, VBG with lactate, coagulation, blood cultures before antibiotics, and LP. Justifies CT before LP by his immunosuppression, while stating that the antibiotics must not wait for it.
check.d: Credit if ordered in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

check.x: Gives the eTG empirical regimen adjusted for this patient:

kids.x: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, then 6-hourly
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly, stating that a past non-severe rash with penicillin is not a contraindication to ceftriaxone

Listeria cover because of the corticosteroids, avoiding benzylpenicillin empirically because of his penicillin allergy label and using an alternative (trimethoprim+sulfamethoxazole, with infectious diseases advice)
kids.d: Also accept meropenem with infectious diseases advice.

check.x: Recognises likely adrenal suppression after a month of prednisolone. Does not stop the prednisolone abruptly, notes that the dexamethasone gives glucocorticoid cover while it runs, plans stress-dose cover afterwards and a supervised taper, and monitors glucose.
Gives symptom relief: paracetamol, titrated IV opioid and an antiemetic such as ondansetron, in a dim, quiet bay.

Admits under medicine or infectious diseases (ICU if he deteriorates) with hourly neurological observations and fluid balance. Notifies the public health unit urgently if meningococcal disease is suspected or confirmed (e.g. PCR positive), so that close contacts such as Mia can be given clearance antibiotics within 24 hours.

Explains to Ned in plain words that this is a bacterial infection of the lining of the brain, not COVID (swab negative), and answers his question about Mia honestly: it depends on the germ, and public health will arrange preventive antibiotics if needed.
Safety netting

Sets escalation triggers for the nurses: a fall in GCS or new confusion, seizure, new focal weakness or unequal pupils, a new rash, falling BP, rising HR or any red zone value, and worsening headache or vomiting.
check.d: Credit in the answer to the management question.

check.x: Tells Ned in plain words to tell a nurse at once about a worse headache, feeling drowsy or muddled, a fit, weakness or a new rash.
Mentions follow-up: a hearing test before discharge and a GP plan for the prednisolone.

part2.lead: It is now 17:20. After your assessment the ED registrar arranged a non-contrast CT brain at 16:05 and performed a lumbar puncture at 16:30. If you ordered blood cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics in Part 1, they were given at 15:45. Here are Ned's observations since arrival, his blood results, the CT brain report and his CSF results.
part2.patient:
For the fourth question, the person playing Ned asks these once each as the candidate explains:

  • “So it's not COVID?”
  • “Can Mia catch it? Does she need anything?”

If the candidate uses jargon (meningitis, CSF, Listeria, adrenal), ask: “Sorry, what does that mean?” If told he must stay in hospital, accept it: “I just want to feel better.”

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: Room air throughout. GCS 15 with pupils equal and reactive at every check. No rash seen at any check.
handover.model:
• Read: at 15:20, 16:00 and 16:45 the temperature (38.9 to 39.2 °C) is in the yellow zone. RR, SpO2, BP and HR (112 to 116) are in the white zone, and the triage glucose is 8.6. At 17:10 RR 26, systolic BP 96, HR 126 and temperature 39.4 °C are all in the yellow zone. CRT is 3 seconds and the nurse is concerned. GCS stays 15 with equal pupils.
  • Meaning: his sepsis is getting worse: BP falling, heart and respiratory rates rising, and lactate 3.1 on the gas. No red zone value yet, but four yellow values all trending the wrong way.
  • Changes: yellow zone values call for a clinical review. With this trend he needs senior ED review now, an IV fluid bolus with reassessment, and ICU review. With multiple yellow zone values and nurse concern, calling a rapid response now under local CERS criteria is also appropriate; accept either an urgent senior clinical review or a rapid response call. A rapid response is mandatory if any value reaches the red zone or the GCS falls. Dexamethasone and antibiotics must already be in, or go in now.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: headache 2 days, fever, neck stiffness
Before CT: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, no rash
After LP: GCS 15, pupils equal, vomited once
Rigor, looks more unwell. GCS 15, pupils equal, no rash. Doctor informed

handover.label: Blood results and venous gas
handover.result: Collected 15:45 at cannulation. Blood cultures (2 sets, 15:45): no growth to date. Nasopharyngeal swab collected 15:40.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 19.6 with neutrophils 17.8, CRP 214. Lymphocytes low at 0.6. Venous pH 7.30, bicarbonate 18, base excess -7, lactate 3.1: a lactic metabolic acidosis. Sodium 134 (mildly low), urea 8.6 with a normal creatinine. Glucose 8.9. LFTs, platelets, INR and APTT normal. SARS-CoV-2, influenza and RSV not detected.
  • Meaning: a severe bacterial infection with sepsis and early hypoperfusion. A lactate of 2 to 4 mmol/L is a yellow zone sepsis criterion under SEPSIS KILLS. Prednisolone adds to the neutrophilia and causes the lymphopenia and the raised glucose. The raised urea fits dehydration from vomiting and poor intake. The negative swab answers his COVID worry.
  • Changes: normal platelets and coagulation meant the LP was safe. Give a fluid bolus, repeat the lactate and monitor sodium and glucose (dexamethasone will raise glucose further). Blood cultures continue and may identify the organism.

handover.label: CT brain report
handover.result:
Examination: CT brain, non-contrast, 16:05.

Clinical details: 32-year-old man on oral prednisolone for a month. Two days of worsening headache with fever, vomiting and neck stiffness. GCS 15, no focal signs. ?Meningitis. Safe for lumbar puncture?

Findings:

  • Brain parenchyma: normal grey-white matter differentiation. No focal lesion, mass or abscess. No acute infarct. No haemorrhage.
  • Ventricles and cisterns: normal ventricular size and configuration, no hydrocephalus. Basal cisterns patent.
  • Midline: no midline shift and no herniation. No sulcal effacement.
  • Extra-axial spaces: no subdural or extradural collection. No subarachnoid blood.
  • Bones, sinuses and mastoids: no fracture. Paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells clear.

Conclusion: normal non-contrast CT brain. No mass lesion, haemorrhage, hydrocephalus or features of raised intracranial pressure.
handover.model:
• Read: a non-contrast CT with no mass, abscess, infarct, haemorrhage, hydrocephalus, oedema, shift or herniation. The sinuses and mastoids are clear.
  • Meaning: there is no contraindication to LP, so it could proceed safely. Clear sinuses and mastoids mean no obvious parameningeal source. A normal CT does not exclude meningitis, and CT misses some early subarachnoid haemorrhage, which the CSF helps with.
  • Changes: CT before LP was reasonable because of his immunosuppression, but antibiotics and dexamethasone should not have waited for it. No neurosurgical input is needed.

handover.label: CSF results
handover.result: Ned Wallace. Lumbar puncture 16:30, left lateral position, opening pressure measured. Cell count, biochemistry and Gram stain reported 17:15. Culture pending (final at 48 hours). Bacterial PCR (Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes), HSV and enterovirus PCR pending.
handover.model:
• Read: opening pressure raised at 30 cmH2O. Turbid fluid. WCC 1650 ×106/L, 88% polymorphs. Red cells 4 (minimal). Protein high at 1.8 g/L. CSF glucose 1.4 with a paired plasma glucose of 8.4: the candidate calculates a ratio of about 0.17 (low). Gram stain shows no organisms. Cryptococcal antigen not detected. Culture and PCR pending.
  • Meaning: turbid fluid with a neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose is the bacterial pattern. Viral meningitis gives clear fluid with lymphocytes and a normal glucose. Fungal infection gives lymphocytes with a low glucose and high protein, and the negative cryptococcal antigen argues against it. A negative Gram stain is common, especially after antibiotics, and does not exclude bacterial meningitis. Minimal red cells argue against subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  • Changes: continue full empirical therapy, including Listeria cover, until culture and PCR return. Then narrow with infectious diseases and decide on dexamethasone duration and public health action once the organism is known.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Ned Wallace, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Ned now, here in the emergency department, including what you want the nurses to escalate.
Ned asks you, “Is this COVID, and can my girlfriend Mia catch it?” Please answer him, then tell him what to watch for and the follow-up he will need.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED JMO; Ned Wallace, 32.
  • Situation: bacterial meningitis with worsening sepsis: four yellow zone values at 17:10.
  • Background: 2 days of worsening generalised headache, fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia; recent viral illness; asthma, on prednisolone for a month; penicillin allergy (childhood rash).
  • Assessment: T 39.4, HR 126, BP 96/56, RR 26, GCS 15, no rash, Kernig's positive, no focal signs. WCC 19.6, CRP 214, lactate 3.1 with acidosis: sepsis with hypoperfusion; COVID negative. CT normal. CSF turbid, OP 30, WCC 1650 mostly neutrophils, protein 1.8, glucose ratio 0.17, Gram stain negative: bacterial pattern.
  • Recommendation: please review now; dexamethasone and ceftriaxone given or going in now; Listeria cover with ID advice; fluids; ICU review; admit.

Bacterial meningitis with sepsis, in a patient immunosuppressed by prednisolone: fever, headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and phonophobia, positive Kernig's; bacterial CSF pattern.

  • Viral meningitis: for: recent viral illness, young; against: neutrophilic CSF with low glucose.
  • Encephalitis: against: no confusion, drowsiness, seizures or focal signs.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: for: onset 'out of nowhere'; against: not thunderclap, not worst-ever, fever, normal CT, minimal CSF red cells.
  • Migraine: for: past migraines, photophobia, phonophobia; against: fever, meningism, constant and different from usual.
  • Tension-type headache: for: dull generalised ache; against: fever, meningism, vomiting.

1. ABCDE assessment; senior ED doctor now for the yellow zone trend (a rapid response call under local CERS criteria is also appropriate); IV crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL to 1 L Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 to 30 minutes, per the local sepsis pathway) with reassessment of BP, HR, CRT, urine output and lactate; ICU review.
  2. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic (now if not given), then 6-hourly.
  3. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly; non-severe rash is not a contraindication.
  4. Listeria cover (corticosteroids): because of his penicillin allergy label, avoid benzylpenicillin empirically and use trimethoprim+sulfamethoxazole (eTG weight-based IV dose, maximum 320+1600 mg 6-hourly), with infectious diseases advice.
  5. Steroid cover: do not stop prednisolone abruptly; dexamethasone covers while it runs, then stress dosing and a supervised taper; monitor glucose.
  6. Paracetamol, titrated IV opioid, ondansetron; dim quiet bay.
  7. Admit under medicine or ID; hourly neuro obs, fluid balance, sodium; narrow therapy once culture and PCR return; notify public health urgently if meningococcal disease is suspected or confirmed, so close contacts such as Mia get clearance antibiotics within 24 hours.
  8. Escalation triggers for nursing staff: fall in GCS or new confusion, seizure, new focal weakness or unequal pupils, new rash, SBP <90 or any red zone value, rising HR or RR, worsening headache or vomiting; call a rapid response for any of these.

• Not COVID: the swab was negative; this is a bacterial infection of the lining around the brain (meningitis), probably more likely because the prednisolone lowers his defences. It needs antibiotics through a drip in hospital.
  • Mia: depends on the germ, known in 1 to 2 days; if it is meningococcus, public health will arrange preventive antibiotics for her; students are usually not close contacts.
  • Tell a nurse straight away: worse headache, feeling drowsy or muddled, a fit, weakness, a new rash.
  • Follow-up: a hearing test before discharge; a GP plan for the prednisolone.

ddx.dx: Bacterial meningitis with sepsis (organism pending; Listeria possible on corticosteroids)
ddx.for: Two days of worsening headache with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and positive Kernig's sign in a man on prednisolone, with turbid neutrophilic CSF, high protein and a low glucose ratio.
ddx.against: The Gram stain shows no organisms, but that is common, especially after antibiotics.

ddx.for: He is young, had a recent viral illness from children at school, and has fever with meningism.
ddx.against: His CSF is turbid with neutrophils, a high protein and a low glucose, and he has a CRP of 214 with a raised lactate.

ddx.for: He has fever and headache and says it is 'affecting the way I think'.
ddx.against: He is oriented with GCS 15, intact attention, no drowsiness, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs.

ddx.for: The headache came on suddenly out of nowhere, with neck stiffness and vomiting.
ddx.against: It was not a thunderclap or worst-ever, with no collapse, and has built over 2 days with fever; the CT is normal and the CSF has minimal red cells.

ddx.for: He has a history of migraines, and this headache is worse with light and noise and better in a dark quiet room.
ddx.against: He has a fever and meningism, and the headache is generalised, constant for 2 days and different from his usual migraines.

ddx.for: The headache is a dull, generalised ache.
ddx.against: He has fever, vomiting, photophobia and marked neck stiffness, and no stress or band-like tightness.

guide:
This is an acute station. In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations and glucose when asked, and give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate names each system, as a block. Ned gives the prednisolone and allergy details only when asked. If an antibiotic is ordered before allergies have been asked about, the nurse asks “Has he got any allergies?” Credit item 13 only if the candidate asked before ordering. If a CT is requested, the nurse asks once whether to wait for it before antibiotics; credit the answer under items 32 and 34. Item 32 is credited only for orders made during Part 1. If the candidate has not ordered anything by halfway, give the nurse's prompt. If results are requested, say they come in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over all four results together, then ask the four questions in order. Credit item 41 (nurse escalation triggers) from the answer to the third question. For item 25, accept either an urgent senior clinical review or a rapid response call at 17:10. For the fourth question, the person playing Ned asks the questions in the Part 2 script. Accept trimethoprim+sulfamethoxazole for Listeria cover without a dose, or meropenem with infectious diseases advice. Also accept a candidate who says benzylpenicillin should be avoided because of his allergy label and that they would seek infectious diseases advice for an alternative. A candidate who prescribes benzylpenicillin without addressing the allergy does not earn item 35.3.

A high-performing candidate soon recognises fever with meningism. They ask about a rash, screen the dangerous and primary headaches in clusters, and uncover the ongoing prednisolone and the nature of the penicillin reaction. They examine the skin, meningism, GCS, pupils and fundi, and order blood cultures, dexamethasone and ceftriaxone before the CT. In Part 2 they see the worsening yellow zone trend, read the CSF as bacterial despite the negative Gram stain, and add Listeria cover with a non-penicillin agent. They also think about adrenal suppression.

A borderline candidate takes a long unfocused headache history, misses the steroids or the allergy, or does not examine for meningism or rash. They wait for the CT or LP before antibiotics, leave out dexamethasone, call the CSF “abnormal” without a pattern, or give benzylpenicillin without addressing his penicillin allergy label.
explain:
Diagnosis: bacterial meningitis in a patient on corticosteroids

Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting are the classic picture of meningitis. Ned has all of them, after a week of a viral-type illness caught from children at school. Kernig's sign (resistance to knee extension with the hip flexed) and Brudzinski's sign (hip and knee flexion when the neck is flexed) support the diagnosis, but they are insensitive. Their absence never excludes meningitis. The key extra feature is that Ned has been taking oral prednisolone daily for a month since his asthma admission, with no plan to stop. This makes him immunocompromised. It widens the list of likely organisms to include Listeria monocytogenes, it is a relative indication for CT before LP, and it means his adrenal axis is probably suppressed.

The headache history: red flags and differentials

Headache red flags: thunderclap onset, fever, meningism, focal deficit, a new headache over 50, a progressive headache, seizures, features of raised intracranial pressure, confusion, pregnancy and immunodeficiency. Ned has fever, meningism, a progressive course and immunosuppression. Ask cluster questions for each cause:

  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: thunderclap onset, maximal within a minute, often the worst-ever headache, sometimes with collapse. Ned's headache came on 'out of nowhere' but was not instantaneous, is no worse than his worst migraines, did not cause collapse, and has built over 2 days with fever.
  • Encephalitis: confusion, drowsiness, behaviour change and seizures. 'Affecting the way I think' turned out to mean poor concentration from pain, and he is oriented with intact attention.
  • Stroke or TIA: sudden focal weakness, speech or visual loss. He has none.
  • Space-occupying lesion and raised ICP: morning or positional headache, vomiting and focal signs.
  • Primary headaches: migraine (his usual ones are one-sided and throbbing, with aura, and do not cause fever), tension-type (band-like) and cluster (unilateral orbital pain with autonomic features). These are diagnoses of exclusion when fever and meningism are present.
  • Others: temporal arteritis (over 50) and trauma.

Antibiotics first; CT before LP only for a reason

When bacterial meningitis is suspected, take blood cultures and give dexamethasone and antibiotics immediately. Never delay them for imaging or LP. A CT brain is needed before LP when there is reduced or falling consciousness, focal neurological signs, seizures or papilloedema. Many protocols add immunocompromise, as here. Ned's normal CT meant the LP could go ahead safely.

Interpreting the CSF

CSFBacterialViralFungal or TB
AppearanceTurbidClearClear or slightly cloudy
White cellsHigh, polymorphsRaised, lymphocytesRaised, lymphocytes
ProteinHighNormal or mildly raisedHigh
Glucose (CSF:plasma ratio)LowNormalLow
CulturePositiveNegativeSpecial stains or antigen

Ned's CSF is turbid, with a raised opening pressure, a neutrophil pleocytosis, protein 1.8 g/L and a glucose ratio of about 0.17: a bacterial pattern. A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis, especially once antibiotics have started. Culture and PCR still identify the organism in many cases. A negative cryptococcal antigen argues against fungal meningitis, which is relevant in a patient on steroids, and minimal red cells argue against subarachnoid haemorrhage.

His bloods show sepsis with a lactic acidosis; a lactate of 2 to 4 mmol/L is a yellow zone sepsis criterion under SEPSIS KILLS. The raised urea fits dehydration from vomiting and poor intake. The glucose of 8.9 and the lymphopenia fit prednisolone. Normal platelets and coagulation meant the LP was safe. His observations show sepsis getting worse (four yellow zone values with nurse concern), which needs senior and ICU review. The negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR answers his main concern.

Management (eTG Antibiotic: Meningitis)

  • Resuscitate and escalate: ABCDE assessment, IV access, IV crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL to 1 L Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 to 30 minutes, per the local sepsis pathway) with reassessment of BP, HR, CRT, urine output and lactate, and senior ED and ICU review. With multiple yellow zone values and nurse concern, calling a rapid response now under local CERS criteria is appropriate; a rapid response is mandatory for any red zone value or a fall in GCS. Give analgesia and an antiemetic.
  • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, then 6-hourly for 4 days. The duration is reviewed with infectious diseases once the organism is known; the benefit is clearest in pneumococcal meningitis.
  • Empirical antibiotic: ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly (or cefotaxime).
  • Listeria cover: eTG adds benzylpenicillin for patients at risk of Listeria: those who are immunocompromised (including on corticosteroids), over 50, pregnant or alcohol-dependent. Ned qualifies, but he has a penicillin allergy label. A childhood maculopapular rash without systemic features is a non-severe, low-risk reaction, so a cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone can still be used. Because of his penicillin allergy label, avoid benzylpenicillin empirically and use trimethoprim+sulfamethoxazole for Listeria cover (eTG weight-based IV dose, maximum 320+1600 mg 6-hourly), with infectious diseases advice.
  • Vancomycin is added when Gram-positive diplococci are seen (possible resistant pneumococcus) or when LP cannot be performed. Aciclovir is added if encephalitis is suspected.
  • Admission: under medicine or infectious diseases (ICU if he deteriorates), with hourly neurological observations, fluid balance and sodium monitoring. Narrow to directed therapy when culture and PCR return.

Steroids and the adrenal axis

A month of daily prednisolone can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so in severe illness Ned may be unable to mount a stress cortisol response. eTG adds Listeria cover for any systemic corticosteroid use, but the dose matters for adrenal suppression and stress dosing, so confirm it from the discharge summary, community pharmacy or My Health Record. His prednisolone must not be stopped abruptly. While the dexamethasone runs it provides ample glucocorticoid cover. When it stops, he needs stress-dose cover while still unwell, then a planned prednisolone taper with his GP or respiratory physician. Monitor glucose, which both steroids raise. That no one told him when to stop his prednisolone is itself a teaching point: every steroid prescription needs a dose, duration and taper plan.

Public health and contacts

Meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b disease are notifiable. Notify the public health unit urgently if meningococcal disease is suspected or confirmed (e.g. PCR positive), so that close contacts such as Mia can be given clearance antibiotics within 24 hours; notification does not wait for culture. Household and intimate contacts are offered clearance antibiotics, arranged with the public health unit. School students are not usually close contacts. Explain honestly to Ned that whether Mia needs prophylaxis depends on the organism.

Complications and follow-up

Complications include sensorineural hearing loss (the commonest), cerebral oedema, seizures, focal deficits, hydrocephalus and septic shock. In hospital, nurses escalate a falling GCS, confusion, seizures, new focal signs, unequal pupils, a new rash and worsening haemodynamics. Before discharge, arrange a hearing test, GP review with a written prednisolone and asthma plan, a medical certificate for work, smoking cessation support, and referral for penicillin allergy assessment (delabelling); his history is low risk. Tell him to call 000 for a fit, being hard to wake or a new rash, and to come back to the ED for returning fever, headache or neck stiffness.
points: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean meningitis until proven otherwise. Always ask about and look for a non-blanching rash.
Take blood cultures, then give dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or before the first dose of ceftriaxone 2 g IV straight away. Never delay treatment for CT or LP.
Ask exactly what the patient takes and confirm the dose. A month of oral prednisolone makes a patient immunocompromised: add Listeria cover, consider CT before LP, and remember adrenal suppression.

Always characterise an allergy. A non-severe childhood rash with penicillin does not rule out ceftriaxone, but benzylpenicillin is avoided empirically: use trimethoprim+sulfamethoxazole for Listeria cover with infectious diseases advice, and refer for allergy delabelling later.
A bacterial CSF is turbid, with polymorphs, high protein and a low glucose ratio. A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis.
Notify public health urgently on suspicion of meningococcal disease so close contacts get clearance antibiotics within 24 hours. Arrange a hearing test after any bacterial meningitis.
